documentTitle: Six pillars, twenty-two themes — ADEB LONODJI
description: How ADEB LONODJI organises its work: six pillars, twenty-two themes and two cross-cutting units, each mapped to the SDG targets it actually touches.
title: Six pillars, twenty-two themes
lede: ADEB LONODJI organises its work into twenty-two themes grouped in six pillars, supported by two cross-cutting units. Each theme is meant to be led by a coordinator who reports to the membership. This page is the English summary; every theme has a fuller description in French .

sections.html:
Before the list

Sixteen themes out of twenty-two have a coordinator

We would rather say this plainly than let a well-ordered table suggest otherwise: six of the twenty-two themes have no coordinator today. The structure below is what the association has decided to build, not what it already runs. If you are a Bedjond professional, in Chad or in the diaspora, and one of these themes is your field, write to us.

Each theme is set against the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals it actually touches — two or three, no more. For each goal we also give the precise target number: the seventeen goals break down into one hundred and sixty-nine targets, and that is the level at which a mapping means anything — “SDG 5” says nothing, “target 5.2, eliminate violence against women and girls” says exactly what is meant. Hover a badge for the full wording. That alignment is our own reading, not a label awarded by anyone, and it can be corrected.

At target level the answer is more qualified, and we would rather give it ourselves: our themes carry forty-five of the one hundred and sixty-nine targets, and three targets central to development are still not among them. We do not claim adult literacy (4.6), child labour (8.7) or the cost of diaspora remittances (10.c). Child malnutrition (2.2), which we used to cite here, joined Health, Nutrition & Prevention on 29 September 2026. For a rural territory in southern Chad these are front-rank issues, and two of them are already listed among the local problems we track. But none of our themes has put them on its programme, and we will not display a target nobody is working on. Those three are open pieces of work — if one of them matters to you, tell us.

Gender & Women’s Empowerment

Coordinator: Odette Tolmbaye

Women’s empowerment, income-generating groups, leadership training, and an effective presence of women in the association’s own governing bodies. The theme also carries the fight against gender-based violence: domestic violence, forced marriage, imposed levirate and abusive widowhood rites, harassment at school. Chad passed an ordinance in 2025 that punishes these acts heavily — up to ten years’ imprisonment for a forced marriage — and almost no one knows it exists: making it known is already an action.

Health, Nutrition & Prevention

Coordinator: Dr Nestor Alladoumdjim

Prevention campaigns, liaison with health centres, the fight against alcohol abuse — adulterated alcohol above all — and hygiene and sanitation. The theme rests on a published health advocacy brief, tracked indicator by indicator: a maternity unit working day and night with a qualified midwife, a reliable cold chain for childhood vaccination, a basic laboratory to diagnose malaria, typhoid and tuberculosis, an ambulance and an evacuation protocol. Targets 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 rest on that brief, not on a mere intention. Update, 29 September 2026: the theme widens to nutrition — screening young children for malnutrition, feeding pregnant and breastfeeding women, links with the health centres and with the Agriculture, Livestock & Food Security theme.

Social Protection, Children & Inclusion

Coordinator: Solkem Ngarmbatina

A mutual-aid fund for bereavement and illness, emergency support, and particular attention to widows and people with disabilities. With Entrepreneurship & Inclusive Finance, this is the association’s anti-poverty theme — not as a slogan, but as a safety net where a death, an illness or a failed harvest tips a whole family over. Update, 29 September 2026: the theme widens to child protection — birth registration, children out of school, early marriage, in line with the association’s safeguarding policy; emergency aid in the event of a disaster or an epidemic moves to theme 20, Emergencies & Risks.

THEME 20
Open

Emergencies & Risks

Coordinator: to be appointed

Preparing the Bedjond country for crises rather than suffering them: rainy-season floods, epidemics, drought, bush fires, displaced families. Ideas under consideration: mapping flood-prone areas with the villages, a simple contingency plan per canton, an alert network over WhatsApp and community radio, and, when a crisis hits, informing, guiding and recording needs for the State services, the Chad Red Cross and humanitarian agencies rather than duplicating them. Created on 29 September 2026; nothing is committed yet, and no money is collected before the association has an account in its name. It takes over the emergency aid previously handled by Social Protection, Children & Inclusion. Update, 1 October 2026: the theme moves to the new Pillar VI, Infrastructure, Territory & Risks, split from the Human Development & Livelihoods pillar; its number does not change.

Energy

Coordinator: to be appointed

Access to energy in the Bedjond country: grid, mini-grid and solar electricity, public lighting, power for schools, health centres and the town hall — our diagnosis knows of no electrified public facility in Bédjondo today. The theme carries the electricity advocacy brief and follows the State and donor programmes that fund electrification. Created on 30 September 2026; it takes over energy, attached since 29 September to theme 08, which becomes Roads & Urban Planning. Nothing is committed yet.
